la:noun:damnum.html:
damnum (late Lat. sometimes dampnum), i, n.
for daminum, neut. of old Part. of dare, = τὸ διδόμενον, v. Ritschl, Opusc. Phil. 2, 709 sq. Less correctly regarded as akin to δαπάνη. Cf. Müll.;
,
hurt, harm, damage, injury, loss; opp. to lucrum (syn. jactura, detrimentum, incommodum, dispendium. Freq. and class.).
In gen.: hauscit, hoc paullum lucri quantum ei damni adportet,; cf.: si in maximis lucris paullum aliquid damni contraxerit,; (with dedecus, as in ; ; ; et saep.); ; ; ; et saep.: propter damna aut detrimenta aliquos miseros esse,; so with detrimenta,; with jactura,: duarum cohortium damno exercitum reducere, * ; cf. ; ; ; 2, 5, 31 fin.: damnum dare alicui, to inflict upon one (ante-classical), (twice); ; ; : facere,to suffer, sustain, (opp. lucrum); ; ; ; but also,to inflict a penalty,; : capere,; and in the alliterative passage: in palaestram, ubi damnis desudascitur, Ubi pro disco damnum capiam,: accipere,; : pati,to suffer harm,; (but damnum pati, also, to permit, put up with harm, ; ): ferre (a favorite expression of Ovid),; ; ; : contrahere (of disease), et saep.: pervenit ad miseros damno graviore colonos Pestis,; cf. ; 8, 777: damna tamen celeres reparant caelestia lunae,i. e. of the waning of the moon,: naturae damnum,natural defect, —Prov.: damnum appellandum est cum mala fama lucrum, (Ribb.).—
Transf., of persons: hoc ad damnum (i. e. scortum) deferetur,: cf. and 60; ; ; cf. .
Esp. in law.
A fine, mulct, penalty, ; ; ; : quis umquam tanto damno senatorem coegit?: eos (leges) morte, exsilio, vinclis, damno coercent,.—
Freq. in the terms,
damnum injuria (datum), i. e. an injury done to another's beast orslave, for which the lex Aquilia provided compensation, (Caesulenus senex) cum ab Sabellio multam lege Aquilia damni injuria petivisset, ; ; ; .—
Damnum infectum, an injury not done but threatened, and against which the person endangered might require security, ; ; (cf. infectus).

la:verb:damno.gloss: to discredit, find fault, disapprove, reject
senses: to discredit, find fault, disapprove, reject
to sentence someone to a punishment, declare guilty, condemn, damn, doom, convict, judge
la:verb:damno.html:
damno (in vulg. lang. and late Lat. sometimes dampno), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
damnum
.
Gen., to occasion loss or damage to, to harm, damage = damno

afficere: pauperibus parcere, divites damnare atque domare,.—

Esp. [cf. damnum, II.] a judicial t. t., to condemn, doom, sentence one to any punishment = condemno, v. (opp. to absolvere, liberare, dimittere; cf. also condemno, culpo, improbo; common and classical).—Constr. with acc. of person, either alone or with gen., abl., de, in, ad, etc., of the crime and punishment: damnatur aliquis crimine vel judicio, sed sceleris, parricidii, etc., Lachm. ad ; cf. Munro, ad : Zumpt, Gr. § 446 sq.; Roby, Gr. § 1199 sq.
With acc. pers. alone: ergo ille damnatus est: neque solum primis sententiis, quibus tantum statuebant judices, damnarent an absolverent, sed etiam illis, etc.,; : censoris judicium nihil fere damnato nisi ruborem affert, (fragm. ap. ): ego accusavi, vos damnastis, Dom. Afer ap. et saep. —Transf., of things: causa judicata atque damnata, Cic. Rab. perd. 4; .—
With acc. pers. and gen. (criminis or poenae): ambitus damnati,; : furti,: injuriarum,: majestatis,: peculatus,: rei capitalis,; sceleris conjurationisque, Zumpt N. cr., et saep.: capitis,; : octupli,: absentem capitalis poenae,; cf.: crimine falso damnari mortis,.—
With abl.: ut is eo crimine damnaretur,; so, capite,: morte,: tertiā parte agri,: pecuniā,; cf.: Milo Clodio interfecto eo nomine erat damnatus,on that account,; morti (abl.) damnare, , v. Weissenb. ad loc.—
With de: de majestate damnatus,: de vi et de majestate,: de vi publica,; cf. quibus de causis damnati,—(ε) With in or ad: nec in metallum damnabuntur, nec in opus publicum, vel ad bestias,: ad mortem,; ad extremum supplicium,: ; .— (ζ) With ut, .—(η) With quod: Athenienses Socratem damnaverunt quod novam religionem introducere videbatur,, ext. 7: Baebius est damnatus, quod milites praebuisset, etc.,.—(θ) With cur: damnabantur cur jocati essent,.
Transf.
To bind or oblige one's heir by last will and testament to the performance of any act.—Constr. with ut, ne, or the inf.: si damnaverit heredem suum, ut, etc.,; with ne, ; with inf.: heredem dare, etc.,: .
In a non-legal sense, to condemn, censure, judge: (with acc. pers. and gen. or abl.) aliquem summae stultitiae, : damnatus longi Sisyphus laboris,: stultitiaeque ibi se damnet (amator),: damnare aliquem voti (poet. and late Lat., voto, votis), to condemn one to fulfil his vow, i. e. by granting his prayer (not in Cic.): damnabis tu quoque votis,, Serv. and Heyne: voto, Sisenn. ap. : voti,; : voto damnatus,; (cf.: voti, Titin. and Turpil. ap. and 10; ; Turpil. Fr. 128 Ribb.): morti,; cf.: Stygio caput damnaverat Orco,: damnati turis acervi,devoted to the gods below, et saep.; cf. also: quem damnet (sc. leto) labor, Heyne: damnare eum Senecam et invisum quoque habere,to condemn, censure, disapprove,: videntur magnopere damnandi, qui, etc.,: debitori suo creditor saepe damnatur,.—Of inanimate objects, to condemn, reject: ne damnent quae non intelligunt,; cf. ; et saep.—Part. fut. pass. as subst.: quem non puduisset damnanda committere,.
Of the plaintiff, to seek or effect a person's condemnation (rare): quem ad recuperatores modo damnavit Plesidippus, ; : Verrem, quem M. Cicero damnaverat,; ; cf. condemno, no. II., and condemnator, no. II.—Hence,damnātus, a, um, P. a.
Prop., condemned: dicet damnatas ignea testa manus,.—
Meton.(effectus pro causa), reprobate, criminal: quis te miserior? quis te damnatior?: damnati lingua vocem habet, vim non habet, (Ribb.).—
Hateful, wretched: damnatae noctes, (5, 11 M.), 15.

Dardănus, a, um, adj., Dardanian, poet. for Trojan: praeda,: puppis,i. e. of Aeneas, (5, 1, 40 M.): arma,: pubes,: gens,: Troja,; also for Roman, as the Romans were descendants of Aeneas: ductor,i. e. the Roman, Scipio Africanus,.—
Dardănĭus, a, um, adj., Dardanian, poet. for Trojan: gentes, Att. ap. Apul. de Deo Soc. 24 (v. 523 Ribbeck): gens,: Aeneae,; 6, 169; cf. carinae,i. e. of Aeneas,; and pinus, the same,: Anchisae,; : Iulus (son of Aeneas),: Roma,: vates,i. e. Helenus,: advena,i. e. Paris,: senex,i. e. Priam,: triumphus, (3, 6, 1 M): minister,i. e. Ganymedes,, et saep.—
Subst.: Dardănia, ae, f.,
the city Dardania, founded by Dardanus on the Hellespont, S. W. of Abydos (whence its mod. name, the Dardanelles), . Oftener, esp. in Vergil,
poet. for Troja, ; ; ; .—
Dardănĭdes, ae, m., son or descendant of Dardanus: Ilus,.—Absol. for Aeneas, ; .—In plur. for Trojan: pastores,.—Absol. for Trojans, ; 445 et saep.—
Dardănis, ĭdis, f., adj., Dardanian, poet. for Trojan: matres,: nurus,; : Caieta (founded by Trojans),.—Absol. for Creüsa, .
A magician of Phoenicia, ; .—Hence,
Dardănius, a, um, adj., of Dardanus: poet. for Magic, artes, .
A Stoic philosopher otherwise unknown, .

la:adj:Danaus.html:
Dănăus, i, m., Δαναός,
son of Belus, and twin-brother of Aegyptus: he was the father of fifty daughters; he emigrated from Egypt into Greece, and there founded Argos; was slain by Lynceus, after a reign of fifty years,; ; ; ; cf. under no. II. B.—Danai porticus, at Rome, dedicated by Augustus to the Palatine Apollo (726 A. U. C.), famed for its statues of Danaus and his daughters, ; cf. (3, 29, 4 M.); Tibul. 1, 3, 79; .—
Derivv.
Dănăus, a, um, adj. (belonging to Danaus; hence, in the poets, meton.), Greek, Grecian: classes,; cf. rates, (4, 22, 34 M.): flammae,: ignis,: miles,: manus,: res,. Esp. freq.,
Subst. plur.: Dănăi, ōrum, m., the Danai, for the Greeks (esp. freq. of the Greeks before Troy), ; ; (4, 7, 31 M.); et saep.—Gen. plur.: Danaum,; (3, 22, 18 M.); 3, 9, 40 (4, 8, 40 M.); et saep.—
Dănăĭdes, um, f., Δαναΐδες, the daughters of Danaus, the Danaides, who, with the exception of Hypermnestra, murdered their husbands at their father's command, ; ; . The classical poets substitute Danai proles, ; cf. (3, 29, 4 M.): Danai puellae,: Danai genus infame,.—
Dănăĭdae, ārum, m., Δαναΐδαι = Danai (v. no. II. A.), the Greeks, .

la:noun:daps.gloss: A sacrificial or solemn feast, religious banquet.
senses: A sacrificial or solemn feast, religious banquet.
la:noun:daps.html:
daps or dăpis, dăpis (nom. daps obsol. : dapis, Juvenc. ap. Auct. de gen. nom. p. 78.—The
gen. pl. and dat. sing. do not occur, but are supplied by epulae, cena, convivium, q. v.), f.
stem, dap-, Gr. δαπάνη, expense: cf. δεῖπνον; R. da-, Gr. δαίω, to distribute; Sanscr. dapajami, to cause to divide
, a solemn feast for religious purposes, a sacrificial feast (before beginning to till the ground; the Greek προηρόσια, made in honor of some divinity, in memory of departed friends, etc. Thus distinguished from epulae, a meal of any kind: convivium, a meal or feast for company; epulum, a formal or public dinner, v. h. v.).
Prop.: dapem pro bubus piro florente facito... postea dape facta serito milium, panicum, alium, lentim, and 132; fin.: pro grege,an offering for the protection of the flock,; ad fin.: ergo obligatam redde Jovi dapem,: nunc Saliaribus Ornare pulvinar deorum Tempus erat dapibus,: sollemnis dapes et tristia dona,.
Transf. by the poets and post-Augustan prose-writers beyond the sphere of religion, and used of every (esp. rich, sumptuous) meal, a feast, banquet, in the sing. and plur. (in Verg. passim, in Tibul. in this signif. only plur.).—
Sing.: ne cum tyranno quisquam... eandem vescatur dapem, Att. ap. (v. 217 Ribbeck): quae haec daps est? qui festus dies? Liv. Andr. ap. P. (transl. of Hom. Od. 1, 225: τίς δαΐς, τίς δὲ ὅμιλος ὅδʼ ἔπλετο); so Catull. 64, 305; ; ; : of a simple, poor meal, ; . Opp. to wine: nunc dape, nunc posito mensae nituere Lyaeo,; cf. so in plur.,; .—
Plur.: ; ; ; ; et saep.; ; ; ; ; et saep.: humanae,human excrement,.

la:adj:daedalus.html:
† daedălus, a, um, adj., = δαίδαλος,
artificial, skilful (poet. and in postclass. prose).
Act.: Minerva, Enn. ap. Paul. ex Müll. (Fr. Inc. Lib. xxi. Vahl.): daedalam a varietate rerum artificiorumque dictam esse apud Lucretium terram, apud Ennium Minervam, apud Vergilium Circen, facile est intellegere, cum Graece δαιδάλλειν significet variare, Paul. ex Müll.: Circe ("ingeniosa," Serv.), .—
With gen.: verborum daedala lingua,the fashioner of words,; cf.: natura daedala rerum,.—
Pass., artificially contrived, variously adorned, ornamented, etc., δαιδάλεος: tecta (apium), skilfully constructed: signa,: tellus,variegated,; ; ; cf.: carmina chordis,artfully varied on strings,.— * Adv.: daedăle, skilfully, Jul. Val. Res gest. A. M. 3, 86.

damnātĭo, ōnis, f.
